Lodge 01 · Cloud Forest Gateway
Rainforest Lodge
Manu Road · 185 km from Cusco · 600 m asl · Near Chontachaca & Patria
Located on the right side of the Manu Road at the foothill of the Andes, the Rainforest Lodge sits at the perfect transition between mountain and jungle. Recently upgraded with a spacious new dining area and a dedicated hummingbird garden with feeders — often the first extraordinary wildlife encounter of any Manu journey.
Comprising 11 double rooms and 11 twin bungalows , each with a private bathroom. Triple beds are available on request. All beds are fitted with mosquito nets and all bungalows are fully netted for comfort and protection.

Lodge 02 · Amazon Lowlands · Private Reserve
Bonanza Lodge
Right bank · Madre de Dios River watershed · 300 m asl · Adjacent to Manu National Park
Situated at the watershed of the Madre de Dios River in the Amazon lowlands, Bonanza Lodge is part of a 750-hectare private ecological reserve run by the Huamani-Choquepuma family — the family of our co-founder William. Adjacent to Manu National Park, the forest here is among the most pristine in the Amazon.
The reserve encompasses multiple distinct habitats: River-Edge Forest, Secondary Growth, Marsh, Bamboo Forest, Primary Forest and Terra Firme — offering extraordinary wildlife diversity in a single location. A comprehensive trail network (Trochas) provides access to all areas. Bonanza Lodge uses an ECO-Bathroom system for minimal environmental impact.

Lodge 03 · Deep Reserve Zone · Terra Firme
Jaguar Ecolodge
Manu Reserve Zone · Terra Firme primary forest · Minutes by boat from Cocha Salvador
The deepest and most exclusive of our three lodges — Jaguar Ecolodge sits inside the untouched primary forest of Manu National Park's Reserve Zone , one of the most restricted and biodiverse areas on Earth. Only a few minutes by boat from Cocha Salvador oxbow lake, home to a resident family of Giant Otters.
Six brand new cabins built from local materials with modern comforts , each thoughtfully designed for rustic elegance: king-size or twin beds, a table and chair on the private terrace, luggage and clothes rack, and a private bathroom. The dining room offers fresh Peruvian cooking with local ingredients. Vegetarian, vegan and gluten-free options on request.
Wake to the calls of Howler Monkeys each morning. The surrounding forest holds Emperor Tamarin, Goeldi's Monkey, Jaguar, Ocelot and an extraordinary density of bird life.

Exclusive experiences
Beyond the lodge
Unique infrastructure built exclusively for our guests — access unavailable through any other operator in Manu.
Observation Towers
Bonanza Ecological Reserve · 20 metres
Amazon Wildlife Perú has recently completed the construction of two metal observation towers — rising 20 metres above the forest floor — inside the private Bonanza Ecological Reserve. Access available exclusively to our guests.
The first tower stands in a transitional bamboo forest just minutes from Bonanza Lodge, offering panoramic birdwatching over the canopy: toucans, macaws, oropendolas and hundreds of other species at eye level. The second is a 40-minute walk to a river-edge forest, where from the top you can observe animals crossing the dry beach below — peccaries, anteaters, agoutis, jaguars and pumas during the dry season.

About Us — Amazon Wildlife Perú
Our story · Est. 2008
Born from the
forest
Amazon Wildlife Perú was founded by two locals from Manu who believed the people who grow up in the Amazon should be the ones to share it with the world.
2008
Founded
+16
Years operating
3
Private lodges
750 ha
Private reserve
100%
Local guides
Our story
A local idea that
changed everything
Amazon Wildlife Peru is an authentic ecotourism company authorised by SERNANP-PERU as an official tour operator for Manu National Park. We run our own vehicles and boats, own three private lodges, and operate a 750-hectare private ecological reserve — all built from nothing by two people who grew up in the shadow of Manu.
Will met Carmen in 2004. Will was a jungle guide; Carmen was a tourism student. Like many couples, they dreamed of opening a travel agency together in Cusco.
"Why weren't local people involved? They had the resources — the knowledge, the land, the passion."
— William Huamani, Co-founder
The idea took real shape in 2007 when Will volunteered as a park ranger at the Limonal checkpoint. He noticed that only foreign companies were running tours in Manu Park — mostly from America and Europe. Local people, who had the deepest connection with the forest, were excluded from the tourism economy. That observation became the founding principle of Amazon Wildlife Perú.
Another driving force was the growing threat to the Amazon from illegal logging, illegal mining and the expansion of cattle ranching in Madre de Dios. Sustainable tourism, they realised, was one of the most effective ways to protect the forest by generating alternative income for local communities.
Timeline
How we grew
2004
Will and Carmen meet in Cusco. Will is guiding; Carmen is studying ecotourism. They share a dream of running their own expeditions.
2007
Will volunteers as a park ranger at the Limonal checkpoint deep in Manu. The observation that no local operators exist in the park becomes the spark.
2008
Amazon Wildlife Perú starts operations — a small desk in Cusco, limited resources, trekking and camping tours at the Bonanza Reserve.
2011
Amazon Wildlife Perú is officially registered as a travel agency, regulated by SUNARP and SUNAT. First full Manu Reserve Zone programs launched.
2016–2020
Expansion of the Bonanza Ecological Reserve. Construction of the private Tapir Clay Lick platform and first observation tower. Growing international reputation.
2022
Jaguar Ecolodge opens inside the Manu Reserve Zone — the first lodge owned and operated by a local Manu family within the park. SERNANP concession granted.
2024–today
Second 20-metre observation tower completed. Rainforest Lodge upgraded with new dining area and hummingbird garden. 5 expert guides, 3 lodges, growing team.
What we stand for
Principles that guide
every journey
Exclusively local expertise
Every guide, cook and porter was born and raised in the Manu region. Our knowledge of the forest is not academic — it is lifelong. Our guides speak English fluently and use professional-grade optics so nothing escapes your eye.
Genuine responsible tourism
We return all waste to Cusco, prioritise local and Peruvian products, eliminate single-use plastics, and minimise boat fuel consumption wherever possible. Our reforestation programme plants mahogany, cedar and kapok trees in Bonanza Reserve.
Community and forest first
We collaborate with local communities and indigenous peoples, directing revenue towards essential jungle preservation. Our private reserve employs local families who have lived there for generations — making conservation economically viable.
Zero-waste policy — All non-recyclable waste carried back to Cusco for proper disposal
Reforestation — Mahogany, Amazon teak, cedar and kapok planted in deforested areas
Fuel reduction — Manu Biosphere programs designed to minimise boat fuel consumption
Local sourcing — All food ingredients sourced from local and Peruvian producers
Anti-extractive — Tourism revenue directly competes with illegal logging and mining
No single-use plastics — Eliminated across all lodge operations and field equipment
The founders
The people who
built this
Carmen Dávila
Co-founder · Manager
From Paucartambo, Cusco
Carmen studied English at Universidad San Antonio Abad de Cusco before completing a degree in Ecotourism and qualifying as a tour guide. After years working with travel agencies across Cusco, Manu and Peru, she co-founded Amazon Wildlife Perú EIRL and now manages all administrative tasks from the Cusco office.
Her extensive knowledge of the Manu area means she can arrange or create any type of itinerary — and she is quick to respond to any enquiry or quote request .
Office: Calle Triunfo 392, Interior 2nd Floor, Office 202, Cusco · amazonwildlifeperu@gmail.com
William Huamani
Co-founder · Director of Operations · Tour Guide
Born and raised in Bonanza, Manu
Will grew up in Bonanza — the private reserve that would later become the heart of Amazon Wildlife Perú. He studied Ecotourism at the Instituto Superior Tecnológico de Manu and has since participated in research projects on monkeys, macaws and Giant River Otters.
His tours are defined by infectious enthusiasm, deep expertise and a commitment to ensuring every guest leaves with lasting memories. He leads guides in the field and continues to guide himself on specialist programs.
Field equipment: Kowa Spotting Scope TSN 663 · Swarovski EL 10×42 binoculars
Our team
Expert guides,
local roots
Every guide at Amazon Wildlife Perú was born in or near Manu, studied ecotourism formally, and has spent years in the field. They are not just guides — they are naturalists, researchers and conservationists who happen to be extraordinary hosts.
Rivelino LLactahuaman
Tour Guide · Birding Specialist
Kimbiri, Cusco

About Manu — Amazon Wildlife Perú
UNESCO World Heritage Site · Est. 1973
About Manu
One of Earth's last truly wild places — a complete vertical ecosystem from Andean cloud forest to Amazon lowland, protecting species found nowhere else on the planet.
1,000+
Bird species
15,000+
Plant species
200+
Mammal species
1.7M
Hectares
1973
Year established
Welcome to Manu
The most biodiverse
place on Earth
Manu National Park, established in 1973, is a UNESCO World Heritage Site recognised for its unique and internationally acclaimed biodiversity. The Manu Biosphere encompasses Andean Mountain Cloud Forest, Tropical Lowland Forest, the Alto Madre de Dios and Manu river drainage systems — covering an area equivalent to half of Switzerland.
It is subdivided into a National Park and two adjacent zones for tourism and cultural subsistence. Within its heart remain indigenous peoples living untouched by modern society — including the Mashco Piro, one of the last uncontacted tribes on Earth.
Due to the low human population and traditional land use, animals in the park are largely unafraid of humans , allowing for extraordinary wildlife sightings at close range. Manu provides unmatched opportunities to observe species that elsewhere are almost impossible to find.
The journey into Manu itself is a spectacle not to be missed. The two-day trip from Cusco to the Reserve Zone entrance takes you through the Andes Mountains , past pre-Inca ruins, cloud forests and eventually to lush lowland rainforest. Unpaved roads wind past cascading waterfalls, deep gorges and precipices.
Manu has abundant wildlife including Jaguars, Tapirs, Anteaters, Black Caimans and Giant Otters . There are 15 species of monkeys, including the Pygmy Marmoset — the world's smallest monkey — and the nocturnal Night Monkey.
Seasonal dynamics
When to visit Manu
The short answer: any time. There is no season that is inherently better — both the dry and wet seasons offer unique and extraordinary experiences.
Dry Season
Clear skies & active wildlife
April → October
Water levels in the Madre de Dios River fluctuate significantly during this period. Wildlife is most visible — Jaguars patrol the exposed riverbanks, birds nest on sandy beaches, and Black Caimans bask in the sun. The cool "Friaje" winds from Patagonia arrive May–July, dropping temperatures and bringing animals to the water's edge.
The dry season is the best time for Jaguar sightings — the low water levels expose long sandy beaches where cats patrol at dawn and dusk.
27°C–34°C average Best for Jaguars Friaje May–July
Rainy Season
Lush forest & river life
November → March
Heavy rainfall peaks from early to mid-March. Many plant species bloom and fruit during this time , attracting pollinators, birds and primates to the riverbanks. River levels rise, reducing shallow areas and making boat journeys smoother. The rains often clear the skies, resulting in stunning blue vistas.
The spectacular thunderstorms can be a delight to witness from a boat. Animal activity increases after rainfall and birding is exceptional as flowers and fruit attract an extraordinary variety of species.
25°C–32°C average 170–310mm/month Best for birding
Ecosystems & ecological levels
Five worlds in
one journey
The Manu Road descends from the Andean highlands to the Amazon basin, passing through five distinct ecosystems in a single day — one of the most dramatic ecological transects on Earth.
Zone 01
Puna Grassland
3,500 m asl and above
High-altitude grasslands at 3,500+ metres where dry air and temperatures fluctuate dramatically with sun exposure. From September to April, temperatures range from -9°C to 22°C , with occasional snow or hail. A transitional wooded thicket zone around 2,600m supports approximately 450 plant species, with annual rainfall of 500–1,000mm. Here you may encounter the Andean Fox, Gray-tailed Deer, and the elusive Andean Bear .
Zone 02
Elfin Forest
1,650 – 2,200 m asl
Trees reach 25 metres, adorned with orchids and ferns thriving on the walls of deep precipices. Characteristic broad-leaved Araceae and tree ferns dominate. The climate is cool and consistently shrouded in shadows and mist , creating a perpetually damp environment of extraordinary beauty. The transition between elfin forest and cloud forest is one of the most dramatic landscape changes on the Manu Road.
Zone 03
Cloud Forest
600 – 1,650 m asl
Also known as the Fog Forest — constant mist envelops this lush landscape where trees reach 30 metres, covered in orchids and ferns, with small streams and waterfalls throughout. Estimated to harbour at least 200 tree species with a density exceeding 700 trees per hectare. Temperatures range 16°C–25°C. This is the habitat of the Andean Cock-of-the-Rock lek, Golden-headed Quetzal, and dozens of hummingbird species.
Zone 04
Tropical Humid Forest (Lowland)
300 – 600 m asl
The vast Amazonian plain — expansive lowland rainforest with high temperatures and rainfall year-round. The transition from foothills to true lowland is marked by the appearance of Giant Trees, epiphytes, lianas and diverse undergrowth . This zone is accessed via the Madre de Dios River by boat from Atalaya Port, and is where Bonanza Lodge is situated.
Zone 05
Terra Firme · Reserve Zone
Below 300 m asl
The deepest and most protected area — the Manu Reserve Zone , accessible only by SERNANP-licensed operators. Primary Terra Firme forest that has never been logged, home to Jaguar, Giant Otter, Tapir, Black Caiman and 15 species of primates. The oxbow lakes (cochas) of Salvador and Otorongo are among the best Giant Otter viewing sites in the Amazon.
Ready to experience Manu ?
Every tour starts from Cusco and descends through all five ecosystems.

FAQ — Amazon Wildlife Perú
Common questions · Before you book
Frequently asked questions
Everything you need to know before booking your Manu expedition.
Everything you need to know
Frequently asked questions
Can't find your answer here? Contact us directly — Carmen replies within 24 hours.
01
What is the maximum group size on the camping trips?
The maximum size of the group is 10 people per guide . If we have more people (between 11 and 14) we send two guides. If there are more than 14 people we split the group into two independent groups – both with their own boats, guides, cooks and program. The only time they spend together is on the first and second day on the lodges like Rainforest Lodge and Bonanza Lodge.
02
What facilities are there at the campsites, for example, for washing and for toilet facilities, and is the tour luxury?
We find it important to minimize our impact as much as possible. Therefore, we do not promote this as a luxury tour. On the contrary, you may encounter some physical hardships such as heat, humidity, biting insects, plus basic washing and toilet facilities.
Jaguar EcoLodge offers clean private toilets, freshwater showers, and a spacious dining area. We also provide a laundry area and a well-maintained garden, with wildlife in the surrounding environment.
03
What type of boats are used for the tours?
The boats are metal-made and feature reclining seats . Life jackets are also provided. The boat has a roof for protection against sun and rain, although rain may still enter from sides while the boat is in movement. In rainy weather, we provide long plastic rain covers for additional protection.
04
Is all drinking water provided?
We provide mineral water for drinking and brushing your teeth . Please bring your own water for the first day, as the tap water at our lodges is not safe for drinking. We recommend taking water bottles for refilling.
05
What is the food like?
Our meals are not all typical Peruvian food, neither normal typical tourist food. It is food that lasts in the heat and humidity of the tropical rainforest. For breakfasts there are fruit salads, omelets, scrambled eggs, pancakes etc. The lunches include juices, since it is usually hot at that time of the day, and the dinners feature soups (the great Peruvian soups!), a main course with meat for the first part of the tour and beans or lentils for the second part (since meat cannot be kept cool for a long time) and desserts of fresh fruits or puddings etc. We don't offer beer nor any alcohol drinks.
We can offer you special diets , such as vegetarian, vegan or any kind of diet according to your request.
06
How is the camouflaged house (hide) or Tapir clay lick?
This is a long wooden made platform, with a roof and stairs with handrails, at about 6 meters high from the ground . This hide or blind is located in the middle of the jungle — there is no bathroom, and we use the bushes for pee. Because it is considered a wildlife area, we do have some local regulations, like not smoking, not using DEET, and staying in silence. For sleeping we provide mattresses and mosquito nets.
07
Why do I need a sleeping bag?
You need to bring a sleeping bag for the night when you sleep at the camouflaged house — light sleeping bags or a simple blanket are enough because of the warm weather.
08
How is the weather during the trip?
The first night we spend at Rainforest Lodge at 600m, where temperatures are about 25 degrees Celsius . In Manu's lowland forest, the temperature at night is normally around 27 degrees Celsius and during the day about 32 to 36 degrees Celsius. However, cold winds from Patagonia may reach Manu National Park and the temperature may lower to about 10 degrees Celsius. These "friajes" are more common during the southern hemisphere's wintertime (between April and the end of June).
09
Is there a lot of walking?
There is not a lot of walking in the sense of going far. All walking is done slowly . This is because most of what you find in a rainforest is vegetation and to be able to pick out the animals you have to take your time to look around, and listen as well. During your trip to Manu National Park, walking is very important in order to find animals. In the Reserved Zone there are trails around the lodges that can last 3 hours maximum. Finally, night walks can be added to most days depending on the lodge area and the activities.
10
Should I take a malaria prophylaxis?
Yes, it is generally recommended to take malaria prophylaxis when visiting Manu National Park. While the risk of contracting malaria is relatively low, especially in certain areas of the park, it's still advisable to take precautions. Consult with a healthcare professional for specific recommendations based on your health and the duration of your stay. Additionally, using insect repellent and wearing long sleeves in the evenings can further reduce your risk.
